message:
* Keep only the beginning and the end of a long token for error messages

For "last read" in parse errors, the lexer keeps the text of the token it
reads. The token start moves only at strings and numbers, so everything
after a string or number belongs to it until the next one starts. Input
that cannot be read again copies that text while parsing (the istream and
FILE* adapters in their carry buffer, the lexer in token_string for
iterators), so valid input of 1 followed by 100,000,000 newlines peaked
at about 225 MB, and a long string was kept a second time.

Replace the carry buffer and token_string by token_text_buffer, which
keeps the first 4096 and at least the last 4112 characters of a token and
drops the characters in between where it would otherwise grow, so
appending stays as cheap as before. get_token_string() shows a token of
more than 8192 characters as its first and last 4096 characters around
"...", the same for every kind of input; contiguous input copies only
these parts.

The example input now peaks at 1.8 MB. Instruction counts of parsing
from std::string, std::istream and FILE* are unchanged (clang 21 and
GCC 15); parsing from std::list<char> needs 1 to 17 % fewer.

Fixes #6120.

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
* Make unflatten() linear in the length of the keys

unflatten() decides in a first pass which prefixes of the keys denote arrays
(those that have a reference token 0 among their children), and looks up
prefixes again in the second pass. A prefix was identified by hashing it, and
by comparing it byte by byte with the entry in the set, from its beginning.
A key with n tokens therefore cost n^2/2 bytes: 100,000 tokens "/0" took
2.4 s (3.12.0: 5 ms), and so did "/0" followed by "/1" tokens, because every
new level looks its prefix up. Keys in the order of an unsorted object type
(ordered_json) defeated the shortcut for keys that share a beginning with the
previous one: four keys were enough to be quadratic.

Prefixes of less than 64 bytes are kept in a hash table and compared as
before, which costs a bounded number of bytes. Longer prefixes are kept in a
tree whose nodes are looked up by their parent and the text of one token. The
node of a prefix is found by walking the tokens of the key from the root, so
all prefixes of a key together cost one pass over the key, and no prefix is
compared as a whole. The nodes along the key walked last are kept, so keys
that share a beginning do not walk it again. The array/object decision and
the independence from the order of the keys are unchanged.

The hash function is seeded with a value derived from the address of a local
variable, which address space layout randomization changes between
processes, so keys cannot be crafted to collide in advance: with the fixed
constants, 20,000 keys of 16 + 2 bytes with the same hash took 0.5 s (random
keys, and 3.12.0: 7 ms). Where addresses are not randomized, or when the seed
is known, k short prefixes can still collide and cost k^2 / 2 comparisons of
fewer than 64 bytes. Results do not depend on the seed.

Measurements (Apple clang -O2, arm64), unflatten() of one key with n tokens:

  tokens "/0"          n=25k  n=50k  n=100k  n=200k
  before              175 ms 617 ms 2437 ms 9729 ms
  after                 4 ms   6 ms   12 ms   27 ms
  3.12.0                1 ms   3 ms    5 ms   10 ms

  "/0" then "/1"       n=25k  n=50k  n=100k  n=200k
  before              153 ms 603 ms 2436 ms 9678 ms
  after                 1 ms   3 ms    5 ms   10 ms
  3.12.0                1 ms   3 ms    5 ms   11 ms

  ordered_json, 4 keys /0*m/a0, /10, /0*m/a1, /11
                       m=25k  m=50k  m=100k  m=200k
  before              397 ms 1402 ms 5191 ms 20723 ms
  after                 4 ms   7 ms   15 ms   33 ms
  3.12.0                2 ms   3 ms    8 ms   17 ms

Ordinary documents (flatten() then unflatten(), instructions retired): within
0.3 % of before for canada, citm_catalog, twitter, jeopardy, mesh,
update-center and random from the benchmark corpus.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Fix -Wuseless-cast in array_prefix_set::reseed

uintptr_t is already uint64_t on LP64 Linux, so the explicit cast is
useless there; rely on the implicit (widening) conversion instead.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Throw type_error.313 when an unflatten key is a prefix of an earlier key

With an object type that keeps the insertion order (ordered_json), a key
such as "/a" can come after "/a/b". The final assignment then replaced the
object built for "/a/b" without an error, so {"/a/b":2,"/a":1} gave
{"a":1}. json never saw this because std::map visits the shorter key first.

Throw type_error.313 if the target of the final assignment is no longer
null, as json does for the same members. A null value keeps the container,
so {"/a/b":2,"/a":null} gives {"a":{"b":2}} for both object types.

Fixes #6105.

message:
* Bound the total number of valueless UBJSON elements per input

An optimized UBJSON array of type Z, T or F has no payload, so its
declared count is not bounded by the input. The limit of 1048576 applied
to each array on its own, so 9 bytes (`[$Z#l` and a count) produced
1048576 values and every further 9 bytes another 1048576: 362 bytes
allocated 661 MB in a DOM, and a SAX handler received 1M events per 9
bytes.

The reader now adds the counts of all such arrays of one input and
rejects the input with out_of_range.408 when the sum exceeds 1048576
plus 4 for every byte read so far. The base is the per-array limit, so
an array that was accepted on its own before is still accepted at the
start of an input. These arrays add about 80 bytes of memory per input
byte (measured 77; one `Z` per byte needs 32), plus the base; the memory
of a document as a whole is not bounded by this. The check runs once per
valueless array, before its start event, with plain size_t arithmetic
that cannot overflow for a 32-bit size_t. Containers with a payload type
and objects (every member needs a key) are bounded by the input already
and are unchanged. BJData rejects these types.

to_ubjson counts the elements of the typed arrays it writes in one call
and writes an array in the unoptimized form (`[#n Z Z ...`) once it would
bring the total above 1048576, which a reader accepts at any input size.
The check is made only for a typed array of a valueless type, so BJData
and other arrays do not pay for it. Everything to_ubjson writes in
version 3.13.0 can therefore be read back.

Two consequences:
- to_ubjson output changes for values with more than 1048576 elements in
  arrays of type Z, T or F: such an array is written at one byte per
  element, e.g. 270000 rows of 100 nulls take 26.8 MB instead of 1.35 MB.
- Output of version 3.12.0 and earlier (typed arrays without such a
  total) is rejected by from_ubjson when the arrays hold more than
  1048576 elements plus 4 per byte of input. 3.12.0 writes a row of up to 255 nulls in 5 bytes (6 above
  255), so a table is rejected from 1075 rows of 1000 nulls or 209723
  rows of 25 (accepted: 1000 rows of 1000, 209000 rows of 25); rows of
  20 or fewer are never rejected.

Measured on the test data: no file of json_test_data (converted with
to_ubjson in all three modes, 846 round trips) holds an array of this
kind with more than 0.17 values per byte. All of them are read back.

Reproducer (K arrays of 1048576 nulls), Apple clang -O2:
  K=40 (362 bytes): before 41943040 values, 664 MB; after rejected, 33 MB
  K=2 (20 bytes):   before 2097152 values, 53 MB;   after rejected, 33 MB

The new tests count events with a SAX handler where they can: building
and comparing million-element values made the first version take 176 s
under Valgrind, the current one about 22 s.

Behaviour change: an input that holds more than 1048576 elements in
arrays of type Z, T or F at more than 4 per byte is now rejected.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Report an empty array for UBJSON [$N#<n>] instead of n elements (#6079)

* Report an empty array for UBJSON `[$N#<n>` instead of n elements

A no-op (N) is not a value, so an optimized array of type N holds no
element whatever count it declares. The reader skipped the elements but
still passed the declared count to the SAX parser: a handler was told
start_array(n) and no element followed, and the DOM parser reserved
min(n, 16384) values (256 KB) for an array that stays empty. Nine bytes
(`[$N#l 0x7FFFFFFF`) therefore committed 256 KB: 2000 of them in one
input, 18 KB, committed 512 MB of heap (capacity 163,840,000 values for
the 10000 arrays of the original probe: 2.6 GB for 70 KB of input).
Untouched pages keep the resident size small, but the commit charge and
a 32-bit address space are consumed.

The reader now announces 0 elements for an optimized array of type N.
The loop that skips the elements is unchanged (it never ran). A count
that does not fit into std::size_t is still rejected by the count
reader; a count that is too large for the array type of the DOM (before:
out_of_range.408 "excessive array size" from the DOM handler) is
accepted now, because the array is empty.

Behaviour change: sax_parse reports start_array(0) for `[$N#n` (before:
n); from_ubjson no longer throws out_of_range.408 for an N-typed array
whose count exceeds the maximum size of the array type.

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
A BON8 string ends at the first byte that cannot continue it. When a
string ends a value and is not terminated by 0xFF, that byte belongs to
whatever follows the value, but the reader has already taken it from the
input and keeps it in its push-back buffer. With strict = true the
end-of-input check reports it; with strict = false the buffer was
discarded, so a following value in a stream lost its first byte or bytes
without an error ({0x61, 0x90} read "a" and then dropped the 0 that
follows).

Report parse_error.110 "string at the end of the value is not terminated
by 0xFF" when the push-back buffer is not empty once a BON8 value is
complete and strict is false, as bon8.md requires the final 0xFF. Output
of to_bon8 always has it, so canonical input is not affected.

Fixes #6110.

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
The seven serializer helpers marked JSON_HEDLEY_ALWAYS_INLINE are inlined
at -O0 as well, and GCC and Clang give every inlined copy its own stack
slots there. That made the recursive frame of dump_container() 2304 bytes
with Clang 21 (2048 with GCC 16), against 480 bytes in 3.12.0, so dump()
of a value nested beyond the default recursion depth limit needed 288 KiB
of stack in an unoptimized build and crashed in a 128 KiB musl thread.

Define JSON_INTERNAL_SERIALIZER_INLINE as JSON_HEDLEY_ALWAYS_INLINE when
__OPTIMIZE__ (or _MSC_VER) is defined and as plain inline otherwise, and
use it for these helpers. The frame drops to 320 bytes and dump() needs
48 KiB at the default limit. The -O2 object code is unchanged with Clang 21
and GCC 16.

Update the stack tables in json_recursion_depth_limit.md and
untrusted_input.md: copying and conversion are now the most demanding
operations at -O0.

Fixes #6116.

message:
* Read a std::u8string from a JSON string and store it as one in every configuration

In C++20, json(std::u8string) was stored as a JSON string only when
std::filesystem::path support was available (the to_json overload sat
inside the JSON_HAS_FILESYSTEM guard), and there was no matching
from_json, so get<std::u8string>() threw type_error.302 ("type must be
array, but is string"). Without std::filesystem, the same expression
still produced an array of code units (the 3.12.0 behavior).

Move the to_json overload out of the filesystem guard so that a
std::u8string is a string in every configuration, build the value
directly from the code units (this also works for a custom string_t
such as the tests' alt_string), and add a from_json overload that reads
a JSON string. The array of numbers written by 3.12.0 is still accepted;
other types throw type_error.302 ("type must be string or array").
std::u8string_view and char8_t arrays are unchanged.

The tests now run in C++20/23 (the file mentions JSON_HAS_CPP_20/23),
also without std::filesystem (test-conversions2_no_filesystem), and with
ordered_json and a custom string type. The new behavior is documented.

message:
Two views compared equal when the tokens of two floats were equal, and
the same node was equal to itself. An edit writes a NaN as the token
"nan", so a view of it (or of an array holding it) was equal to itself
and to another NaN, while json(NaN) == json(NaN) and view == json are
false. The token shortcut now excludes the edited "nan" token (found by
the missing digit layout), dispatched on the document mode by a tag: a
read-only document cannot hold a NaN, and its walk is unchanged
(instruction count and cycles on canada, citm and twitter within
noise). For editable documents the check costs about 2 % instructions
on canada (cycles within noise). The same-node shortcut is kept for
read-only documents and for editable ones that were never edited; a
document with edits is walked, so comparing it with itself is linear
instead of constant.

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
* Read iterator pairs of std::string and std::vector as pointer ranges

Before C++20, a pair of iterators of a contiguous container cannot be told
from any other random-access iterator, so json::parse(s.begin(), s.end())
on a std::string or std::vector<char> was read one character at a time,
without the bulk scans of strings, numbers and indentation that the
container itself gets (the container overload of input_adapter() already
maps it to a pointer range). The iterators of std::string and of a
std::vector of 1-byte integral elements are now matched exactly and mapped
to the pointer range they cover; an empty range is not dereferenced. The
character type stays the same, so the results and error positions do not
change.

parse(first, last) of a std::string gets 1.7-2.0x as fast in C++17 on an
Apple M1 Max, accept(first, last) 2.7-3.1x, and from_cbor(first, last) of a
std::vector 8-23% faster.

message:
dump() batches float tokens of 16 or 17 digits with at least 8 fraction
digits. A damaged image loaded with image_check::bounds can record a
token with no digit before the point and 17 after it, which no JSON
number has. Its q = -17 is outside the range of locate_token(), which
then read fives[17] past its 17 entries; on x86-64 the resulting digits
had 18 digits and failed the assertion of write_decimal() (OSS-Fuzz
issue 583898810, json_view_image_fuzzer).

The batch now takes 8 to 16 fraction digits, which every valid token of
16 or 17 digits has, so it batches the same tokens of valid documents.

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
* Scan the buffer of a FILE in bulk with glibc and the Apple C library

Parsing from a FILE* still read one character at a time through
getc_unlocked(), while a std::istream has its get area scanned in bulk.
file_input_adapter now offers the lexer the same kind of window into the
buffer of the FILE: it reads the fields that the C library's own
getc_unlocked() macro reads (glibc: _IO_read_ptr and _IO_read_end; Apple:
_p and _r) and consumes exactly the characters getc_unlocked() would
return, so the file is left where it was left before. The part of the
current token in a buffer that is about to be refilled is kept for error
messages, as for streams. The window needs the file locked for the whole
parse, so JSON_DISABLE_UNLOCKED_FILE_IO and MemorySanitizer builds turn it
off; uClibc, which defines __GLIBC__ but has other fields, does not get it.

parse() from a FILE* gets 2.0-2.6x as fast on an Apple M1 Max and 1.7-2.2x
on x86-64 (glibc, GCC 15 and Clang 21), accept() 2.9-4.4x; that is about as
fast as parsing from a std::ifstream. The new tests read with FILE buffers
of 1 to 70 bytes and unbuffered files, after ungetc(), with SAX positions
and with binary strings across the buffer's edges.

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
output_vector_sink grew the vector by resizing it to its whole new
capacity. resize() zeroes the characters it adds, so every doubling
zeroed megabytes of a fresh allocation at once: that faults in all its
pages and evicts them from the cache before the writer reaches them,
and the writer's stores then miss again. The sink now reserves the same
capacity as before but resizes the vector only to 64 KiB
(vector_sink_window) ahead of the position, which is still cached when
the writer's stores come.

to_cbor(), to_msgpack(), to_ubjson(), to_bjdata() and to_bon8() of an
array of one million numbers into a fresh vector: 4-26 % faster on x86
(Skylake laptop with Apple clang 13, Haswell VPS with GCC 16 and
Clang 23), 1-2.5 % on Apple M1 Max; other documents unchanged (within
0.4 % in reruns). The capacity and growth of the vector are as before.

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
* UBJSON/BJData reader: reject a container count equal to SIZE_MAX

The reader marks a container whose count is not known by npos, which
is SIZE_MAX. A count of exactly that value was stored unchanged and
then read as "no count", so the BJData input

    [ # M ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff i 01 ]

parsed as [1] instead of throwing out_of_range.408 as a count of
2^64-2 does. Where size_t is 32 bits, the same holds for 'm' and 'L'
counts of 2^32-1, in UBJSON too.

The counts of 'm', 'M' and the signed types now go through
store_ubjson_count(), which rejects npos with "integer value overflow"
(the message a count beyond size_t already gets), as the CBOR reader
does in get_cbor_container_size(). An ND-array dimension of 2^64-1 gets
the same message now, where it was "excessive ndarray size caused
overflow" (the product check) on 64-bit platforms.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* MessagePack reader: reject an array/map 32 length equal to SIZE_MAX

On a platform with a 32-bit std::size_t, an array 32 or map 32 length of
0xFFFFFFFF equals unknown_size(), so start_array()/start_object() were
told the size was unknown and skipped the max_size() check. Route both
through the CBOR length check, renamed get_container_size(), which
already rejects that value.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
* Make basic_json::insert() provide its documented strong exception guarantee (#5986)

A failed allocation while the new elements were copied left the value
changed, and with JSON_DIAGNOSTICS stale parent pointers behind. The
extra work now happens almost only on the failure path:

- Array insert(pos, cnt, val) and insert(pos, first, last) append the
  copies at the end and rotate them into place. If a copy throws, the
  appended elements are erased again (noexcept) and the parents are set.
  Moving a basic_json cannot throw, so reallocation is safe. This is no
  slower than vector::insert (faster for numbers), needs no temporary
  array, and keeps the elements that libstdc++ lost on reallocation.
- Array insert(pos, val) copies a non-scalar value first and inserts it
  by move, except at the end, where vector::insert is strong. Scalars
  keep the direct path.
- The object range insert(first, last) into an empty object uses the
  container's own range insertion and clears the object on an exception.
  Into a non-empty object it inserts member by member and logs one bit
  per source member (a new member is detected by the size change; no
  allocation for the first 256 members); on an exception the members
  added are erased by walking the source range. No assumption that
  key_type is string_t.
- The parents are set when a failed insertion is undone.

The regression test fails every allocation of every insert() overload in
turn, for json and ordered_json, and checks the value and its parents.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Fix clang-tidy and -Wnrvo findings in insert rollback helpers

Declare the rollback helpers non-movable, replace the nested conditional
and C array in object_insert_rollback, silence the intentional copy in the
allocator test, and avoid the missed NRVO in the test factory lambda.

* insert(): strong guarantee for single elements, basic for the rest

Rework of the previous two commits, following the discussion in #5996:
the standard containers give the strong guarantee only for a single
element (std::vector: at the end, or if the exception does not come from
copying T; std::map: single-element insert), and copying a basic_json
allocates. Rebuilding a rollback for the count, range and object-range
overloads on top of array_t/object_t made the code verbose and slower.

- insert(pos, const basic_json&): at end() forward as before (the
  standard covers it); elsewhere copy first and insert by move, as
  libstdc++ does internally (libc++ shifts the tail before copying).
- insert_iterator() and object insert(first, last) set the parents in a
  scope guard, so a failed insertion leaves a valid value with
  JSON_DIAGNOSTICS too (the next assert_invariant() aborted before).
- Docs: strong guarantee for (1), basic guarantee for (2)-(5); the
  argument checks throw before anything is changed.
- Test: allocation-failure sweep checks the strong guarantee for (1) and

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
* Binary readers: swap the bytes of floats with a single byteswap

byte_swap reversed float and double values byte by byte. GCC does not
merge that loop into one bswap, and C++23's std::byteswap accepts only
integers. Overloads for float and double now copy the bits into a
uint32_t/uint64_t, call detail::byteswap, and copy them back. This
applies to every binary reader that uses get_number.

In the CBOR reader, the single- and double-precision float cases call a
non-inlined helper. Without it, GCC stopped inlining the stream
adapter's get_character() into parse_cbor_internal, which made reading
from a std::istream about 0.5 % slower.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* CBOR reader: inline get_cbor_float() and always inline get() instead

The never-inlined get_cbor_float() costs a call for every float read
from input without bulk access: reading canada.json from CBOR through a
FILE* became 5.6 % slower on Apple clang in the benchmark suite. The
helper existed only because GCC 13 stopped inlining the stream adapter's
get_character() into parse_cbor_internal. Always inlining
binary_reader::get() fixes that as well.

callgrind, all binary formats on buffer, std::istringstream and FILE*
input (canada and citm_catalog): GCC 13 0.986-1.003, GCC 16 0.994-1.006,
Clang 23 identical. Apple clang suite: FromBinaryFile/cbor/canada 0.939,
geomean of the 53 binary reader rows 0.998.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

message:
* Compare json_view values without a vector per container and a basic_json per number

operator== of views (view/view, view/json, and editable documents) built two
vectors of members for every object it entered, sorted them with stable_sort
for every object, and converted each number to a basic_json value. It now:

- keeps the members of all open objects in one vector (reserved with
  geometric growth, so that nested objects do not reallocate), and orders
  them by insertion sort for up to 16 members, or not at all when the keys
  ascend already;
- compares numbers of one type directly, and builds a basic_json only for
  numbers of different types;
- compares short texts (keys, numbers, most strings) with two overlapping
  loads (bytes_equal(), in node.hpp);
- first walks both documents in lockstep, in the order of their text, which
  finds most pairs of equal values without the work of the comparison. The
  walk only enters an object if the comparison would visit its members in the
  same order (the object type keeps the order, the keys ascend, or all values
  are scalars), so a difference is never found later than before, and it
  records the containers it found different, so that the comparison does not
  walk them again;
- rejects values of different types and arrays of different sizes before any
  of this, and, for an object type that keeps the order, objects whose first
  (up to four) members have different keys, which ends a comparison that
  differs near the start without preparing the members.

Results are unchanged: numbers compare by value across types, duplicate keys
resolve as parse() resolves them, and objects compare in document order for
ordered_json and by key otherwise.

(develop -> now), json_document / ordered_json_document / editable:

A sweep that places one difference at about 2,100 positions of eight

* Check the float tokens of a json_document image without a sort and a scan of every character

load(image_check::full) checked every float token of an image by sorting
the token ranges, scanning the token character by character, and comparing
the digit layout with the node's. Now:

- the ranges are sorted only if they are not sorted already (save() writes

- a token of the shape [-]digits.digits whose digit counts are the ones the
  node records (nearly all of them) is accepted by checking its digits eight

* Build the DOM parser with Visual Studio 2015 again

Since #5882, the three VS 2015 jobs of AppVeyor fail on develop:

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
* Keep the value unchanged when operator[] with a JSON pointer throws

The non-const operator[](json_pointer) is documented with strong exception
safety, but get_unchecked created intermediate values while walking the
pointer and kept them when a later reference token failed, e.g.
json j; j["/a/99999999999999999999999"_json_pointer] threw 404 and left
{"a":[]}; padding an existing array or appending with "-" behaved alike,
and so did std::length_error/std::bad_alloc from a huge index.

get_unchecked now only walks existing values up to the last reference
token. The last token's key insertion or array growth is strongly
exception safe by itself. Any other change goes through
get_unchecked_create, which records the one change it makes to an existing
value (null converted, key inserted, array grown) in a RAII guard and
reverts it if a later step throws; everything else it creates lies below
that change. The guard needs no try/catch, so JSON_NOEXCEPTION builds are
unaffected. Successful calls create the same values as before.

Docs: state the guarantee in the exceptions list and version history of
operator[], fix the complexity of the pointer overloads of operator[] and
at, and warn that padding arrays up to an untrusted index allocates memory
proportional to the index (operator[].md, untrusted_input.md).

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Make the strongly exception-safe pointer operator[] faster than before

The previous commit made get_unchecked strongly exception safe but slower
with GCC 16 when it creates values (up to +6 % instructions for appending
with "-"). This restructures it so that no benchmark row is slower than
before the strong guarantee, with GCC 16, Clang 22 and Apple Clang.

- get_unchecked walks existing values in one loop that inserts nothing.
  The last reference token is resolved in that walk: "-" appends with
  emplace_back(), an index grows the array with operator[], and a missing
  key is inserted with emplace_hint() at the position the walk's
  lower_bound() found, so the key is searched once.
- With std::less<string_t> or std::less<> as comparator, the walk checks
  the key at the lower bound for equality instead of equivalence, which is
  the same for these comparators and cheaper.
- get_unchecked_create (not inlined) handles all other changes. Its guard
  swaps a null value with a fresh null value instead of copying it and
  reverts the change in a non-inlined function, so a successful call pays
  one compare for it. As every null value converted afterwards is a fresh
  one, it is converted in place instead of assigning a new array or object.
- Keys are added to new objects with emplace(), which also replaces the
  basic_json::operator[] call for ordered_json.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Fix rollback of pointer operator[] for unusual object and string types

Follow-up to the strong exception guarantee of the non-const
operator[](json_pointer):

- get_unchecked_create assumed that emplace() always inserts the key that
  the walk did not find. For object types whose lookup and emplace()
  disagree (e.g. a copied fifo_map), nothing was inserted, the rollback
  erased the existing member, and the walk continued with a value of the
  wrong type (assertion, type_error.305, or a crash). It now checks the
  result of emplace(), arms the rollback only if a key was inserted, and
  otherwise continues the walk with the member found, as basic_json's
  operator[] does: such pointers throw out_of_range.404 and leave the value
  unchanged, as before the strong guarantee.
- The rollback erased the inserted key by key, which converts string_t to
  object_t::key_type and may allocate inside a noexcept function
  (std::terminate on bad_alloc with custom key types). It now erases by the
  iterator emplace() returned, and shrinks a grown array with erase() at
  the end instead of resize(). The documentation states the remaining
  requirement for custom template parameters.
- Creating values no longer calls string_t::begin(), so the non-const
  operator[](json_pointer) compiles with string types that lack it (as the
  alternative string type of the tests).
- Correct the @throw lists of get_unchecked and get_unchecked_create.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Address review comments on operator[](json_pointer) rollback

- undo() shrinks the array with resize() instead of erase()
- comments say what "will be" done in get_unchecked_create
- tests: avoid a clang-tidy performance-unnecessary-copy-initialization
  hit (unit-alt-string) and the word "access" in section names, which
  Flawfinder flags as race/access

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Let the pointer rollback guard call undo() unconditionally

The check in the destructor and JSON_HEDLEY_NEVER_INLINE on undo() made no
measurable difference: instruction counts of j[ptr] are identical with
GCC 13 -O3 and within 0.4 % with clang, timings are within noise.

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
* Write and read the inner length of BSON binary subtype 0x02

The BSON specification defines the payload of the "binary (old)" subtype
0x02 as an int32 followed by that many bytes. to_bson wrote the plain
payload instead, so decoders such as pymongo and libbson-based readers
rejected the bytes, and from_bson returned the inner length as part of the
payload (documented as lenient behavior in gh-5333).

The writer now emits the outer length (payload + 4), the subtype, the inner
int32 holding the payload size, and the payload. The reader requires an
outer length of at least 4 and an inner length equal to the outer length
minus 4 (the cases the bson-corpus lists as decode errors), reports parse
error 112 otherwise, and returns only the payload. Both directions change
together so that the round trip keeps working.

The single-reservation fast path for scalar entries declines subtype 0x02
because it has no room for the inner length.

This is a deliberate exception to the opt-in rule for behavior changes:
the previous output was invalid BSON.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Check the declared BSON document size before reading its content

The BSON reader compared a document's declared size with the number of bytes
read only when it reached the terminator. The declared size never bounded
the reads, so a SAX handler saw the keys and values of a document whose size
was too small before parse error 112 was reported.

The container frame now stores the position where the document ends
according to its declared size. open_bson_document rejects a size below 5
(size prefix plus terminator) and an embedded document that does not end
before the terminator of its enclosing document; the element loop rejects an
element whose type byte leaves no room for the name terminator and the
document terminator. The terminator check stays and still catches a declared
size that is too large. No input that was accepted before is rejected now;
documents with a wrong size are reported earlier, with fewer SAX events, a
different byte position and, in three cases, a different message. The error
id (parse_error.112) is unchanged and strict=false still does not skip the
check.

The tests that asserted the old messages and positions are updated, with the
outer sizes of two inputs corrected so that they still exercise the embedded
document. New tests cover the SAX events, a size below 5, and an embedded
document that fits exactly.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Document BSON subtype 0x02, document size checks, and lenient reads

Describe the inner length of binary subtype 0x02 that to_bson now writes and
from_bson checks and removes. Add the document size checks (parse_error.112,
not affected by strict=false) to bson.md and from_bson.md, and extend the
list of lenient reads with the UUID and MD5 payload lengths (not checked),

so tokens that can never be a valid array index selected an array and
then failed:

- "01" (and any other token with a leading '0') threw parse_error.106
- the empty token threw out_of_range.404

Both tokens are valid object keys, and both work when the level already
exists as an object, so creating the level changed the outcome. Test the
token against the RFC 6901, Sect. 4 grammar for array indices instead, so
that such tokens create an object. This only affects pointers that threw
before.

The note described valid array indices as "a nonempty sequence of digits
without a leading 0", which read literally excludes the token "0" itself,
contradicting both the code and the /foo/0/0/0 example in the next
sentence. Spell out the RFC 6901 grammar instead.

message:
* Write the indented output of json_view's dump() with the fast writer

The compact writer of dump() (cursor in a register, fixed-size copies of
tokens) served dump(-1) only; every dump(indent), and everything with
ensure_ascii that was indented, went through a generic walk that calls put()
for each token and put_repeated() (a memset call) for each line break. The
fast writer now writes indented output, too, with or without ensure_ascii, and
the generic walk is gone. A line break is a copy of a 64-byte ruler (a line
break and 63 indentation characters) when the line is at most 64 bytes, and a
store plus memset beyond that. The depth is counted only in the indented
instantiations (counting it in the compact one cost an editable document 5 %
with Clang). The indented walks are out of line (dump_pretty()): inlined
into dump() next to the compact ones, they made compact dumps of integer
arrays 7 % slower.

A decoded string (one with escape sequences) of a damaged image loaded with
image_check::bounds can contain invalid UTF-8. As before, the compact dump
writes such bytes unchanged, and the indented dump throws type_error.316; its
runs are found by the lexer's validating scan (a scalar validation of every
sequence made dump(2) of decoded CJK text twice as slow as before).

dump(2) instructions per call, macOS arm64 (before -> after):

               twitter         citm            canada          jeopardy(4k)
  json         3.75M -> 1.85M  8.28M -> 3.93M  67.1M -> 56.0M  9.56M -> 4.81M
  editable     3.82M -> 1.84M  8.48M -> 4.02M  68.1M -> 56.2M  9.66M -> 4.75M

Linux instructions (GCC 13 / Clang 18), dump(2) and dump(2, ' ', true):

  twitter      -25 % / -30 %      -11 % / -11 %
  citm         -29 % / -28 %      -24 % / -24 %
  jeopardy(4k) -25 % / -32 %      -20 % / -24 %
  CJK text with \u escapes  -6 % / -11 %   -2 % / -2 %

The compact dump is unchanged (within +0.4 % on Linux, within noise on the Mac).

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Scan the strings of json_view's dump() with ensure_ascii 16 bytes at a time

With ensure_ascii, a string of the source that has a byte >= 0x7F was written
by a generic path: put() per piece and a validate-and-decode step for every
character beyond ASCII. It now goes through a writer with the cursor in a
local variable. The part of the string that has nothing to escape is found
16 bytes at a time (SSE2 or NEON; the existing 8-byte scan without vector
support) and copied; strings that are ASCII throughout are still decided by
the 8-byte check of dump() with ensure_ascii (a 16-byte scan for them was
2-5 % slower for short strings). The two-byte sequences (lead C2..DF) and
the three-byte sequences whose continuation bytes may have any value (lead
E1..EF except ED) are decoded with a few compares; E0, ED, four-byte
sequences, and damaged input go through validate_one_utf8() as before, so
damaged images still throw type_error.316.

dump(-1, ' ', true) instructions per call, macOS arm64 (develop -> now);
the compact dump without ensure_ascii and dumps of ASCII text are unchanged:

  twitter 5.42M -> 3.57M    citm 3.28M -> 3.24M     jeopardy(4k) 5.78M -> 5.65M
  CJK text, raw 66.5M -> 35.3M    escaped \u 32.7M -> 17.0M
  Latin text with accents 11.5M -> 9.4M    ASCII text 4.40M -> 4.40M

Linux instructions (GCC 13 / Clang 18), dump(-1, ' ', true):

  twitter -9 % / -33 %    CJK text -14 % / -47 %    Latin text -8 % / -18 %
  citm -0.2 % / -0.4 %    ASCII text -0.1 % / -0.3 %

The compact dump without ensure_ascii is unchanged (canada 0.0 %).

The unit test covers every character of the Basic Multilingual Plane, and a
character that needs an escape at each position of strings of 0..40 bytes.

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
* Flatten into a std::map by inserting next to the previous entry

flatten() added every path with operator[], so each insertion into the
std::map of the result searched the tree from the root and compared long
shared path prefixes, which took half the time on canada.json. Paths come
out in nearly sorted order, so they are now inserted with emplace_hint
next to the entry added last, for object types that have it. ordered_map
keeps its append without lookup, and other object types keep
operator[].

Path segments are also appended in place, without a temporary string
for each escaped key or array index.

flatten() of canada.json, citm_catalog.json and twitter.json is 1.4x to
1.9x as fast; ordered_json is unchanged (1.05x). The output is
unchanged.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Unflatten without splitting keys or walking each path from the root

unflatten() split every key into a vector of reference tokens, stored the
pointer prefixes in a tree to decide which values become arrays, and then
looked up every token of every key from the root again.

Keys are now checked by a scan that raises the same parse_error.107/108 as
split(), skipping the part a key shares with the previous one, which was
checked already. The prefixes that denote arrays are kept in a small hash
set of key slices; the array/object decision is unchanged. The walk keeps
the values along the previous key's path, so only the part of a key that
differs from the previous one is looked up. Keys of a flattened object are
usually sorted, so that part is short.

unflatten() of canada.json, citm_catalog.json and twitter.json is 1.9x to
2.3x as fast; the output and the exceptions are unchanged.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Apply plain JSON Patch operations without building a json_pointer

patch() built a json_pointer for every operation, which splits the path
into a vector of strings, and for "add" and "remove" a second one for
the parent. That took 20% to 45% of the time not spent copying the
document.

"add", "remove", "replace" and "test" with a path that has no escapes and
denotes existing values (the parent, for "add"), as diff() creates them,
are now applied by resolving the path in place, reusing one string for
the reference tokens. Every other operation, and every operation that
would fail, takes the existing code, so the results, the exceptions and
the state left after a failing operation are unchanged.

patch() of the diffs of canada.json, citm_catalog.json and twitter.json
is 1.02x to 1.10x as fast; the rest is the copy of the document.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Build diff operations member by member

diff() created every operation from an initializer list, so each
{"op", "replace"} pair became a temporary array with two heap strings
before it was turned into an object member; an operation took about 25
allocations. The operations are now built as objects whose members are
assigned one by one. Paths of members and elements are also built in
place, without a temporary string for each escaped key or array index.

diff() of canada.json, citm_catalog.json and twitter.json, with every
eighth scalar changed, is 1.3x to 1.6x as fast; the output is unchanged.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Diff objects with the same keys in lockstep and keep one path buffer

diff() looked up every key of the source object in the target object,
and built a new string for the path of every value it descended into.
Objects of the same size usually have the same keys in the same order,
so they are now walked together as long as that holds, without a
lookup; objects that differ fall back to the lookup from the first key
that does not match. The path is one buffer that is extended before
descending and shortened again afterwards. Objects whose members are
equal but in a different order (possible with ordered_json) still get
no operations.

Together with the previous commit, diff() of canada.json,
citm_catalog.json and twitter.json is 1.5x to 2.0x as fast; ordered_json
1.65x to 1.85x. The output is unchanged.

dump() now checks strings of up to 32 bytes against a table of the bytes
that can be written verbatim, four bytes per step, and copies them in one
go if all of them can. That is cheaper than setting up the vector scanner,
whose setup costs more than such a string takes to scan; SQLite's
jsonAppendString() writes strings with the same kind of table loop. Most
object keys and many values are this short (citm_catalog averages 8 bytes
per string, jeopardy 14).

GCC 16 and 13 stopped inlining put_indent() and put_literal() into the
pretty-printing loops once dump_escaped() had grown, which made indented
output up to 13% slower; both are now always inlined.

The new test puts every ASCII character and a 2-byte character at every

reference implementation of the existing UTF-8 tests.

* Match literals without a stack array and keep parser states in bytes

scan_after_whitespace() built the expected text of true, false, and null in
local std::array objects. With -fstack-protector-strong (the default of
Ubuntu's GCC, among others), a local array gives the function a stack canary
check, which then ran on every token. scan_literal() now takes the text

parameter; for contiguous input it compares the rest at once and falls back
to the byte loop on a mismatch, so errors are reported at the same
character. It is out of line, which keeps the token dispatch small.

message:

token_buffer (an out-of-line std::string::append) was about 10% of parsing

json_sax::number_float(), and the library's own handlers
(json_sax_dom_parser, json_sax_dom_callback_parser, json_sax_acceptor)
ignore it.

For contiguous input, the fast path now keeps a pointer to the token in the
input, and get_string() copies it on first use. The parser passes an empty

and json::accept() never copy float text. User handlers, and

unchecked get_string_token(). Input read through a window into a stream

refill the window.

message:

message:

inline function that reads the stdio buffer (fp->_IO_read_ptr) directly.

parsers read from a FILE* (e.g., the fuzz harness FILE* leg, OSS-Fuzz
575915982). std::fgetc is an opaque call whose result MemorySanitizer treats
as initialized.

regression from #5828 and not part of any release.

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
* Escape characters below 0x60 from a table straight into the write buffer

When the bulk scanner in dump_escaped_impl() stops at a control
character, a quote or a backslash, that byte used to go through the
UTF-8 decoder and a switch that wrote the escape byte by byte into
string_buffer, which was then copied into write_buffer at the next run.

A byte below 0x60 at a character boundary is a complete code point, so
it now skips the decoder: its escape sequence comes from a 96-entry
table of 8-byte rows (sequence padded with zeros, length in the last
byte), and all 8 bytes are copied straight into write_buffer with one
room check. The check sits inside the existing character-boundary
block, so it runs once per scanner stop and not once per byte; testing
every byte cost about 6% on twitter.json with ensure_ascii.

The switch in the decoder's accept branch lost its cases for
characters below 0x60, which can no longer reach it.

Output is byte-identical. The string-buffer boundary tests now use
\u-escaped non-ASCII characters, since simple escapes no longer reach
string_buffer, and a new test case checks every ASCII character at
every position against a reference escaper.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Avoid raw string literals with backslashes in CHECK macros

MSVC's traditional preprocessor mis-lexes raw string literals inside
macro arguments and reports illegal escape sequences (C2017, C3850).

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Sweep invalid UTF-8 at every position through dump()

Compare dump() of strings with ill-formed UTF-8 (stray continuation
bytes, invalid lead bytes, overlong encodings, surrogates, code points
above U+10FFFF, and sequences cut short by ASCII, a quote, a backslash,
a lead byte, or the end of the string) with an independent reference
serializer, for every error handler and with ensure_ascii on and off.
The pattern is put at every position of short strings to cross the
strides of the bulk scanners, and of longer ones to cross the end of the
512-byte string buffer.

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

message:
* Speed up JSON pointer parsing, formatting, comparison and lookup

Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Restore unflatten() speed after the linear-time rewrite

The prefix tree introduced for linear unflatten() kept a std::map per prefix,
copied each token into it and looked every token up a second time while
creating the values. Replace the per-prefix maps by one open-addressing table
keyed by (parent, token) that refers to the parsed tokens, skip the lookups for
the prefix shared with the previous key (flattened objects are mostly sorted),
and derive the prefix numbers of the second pass from parent links instead of
lookups.

independent of the iteration order of the flattened object.

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
Pretty-printed JSON indents every line with a run of spaces, which
skip_whitespace() read one character at a time. For contiguous input
(bulk_scan) the lexer now skips the spaces after a newline 8 bytes at a
time directly in the input buffer, including the leading spaces of the
last, partial word. This bypasses get(), which is safe because
bulk_scan implies the lazy position from the previous commit: nothing
is counted per character.

Compared to lazy positions alone, pretty-printed input (twitter,
citm_catalog with indent 2 and 4) parses up to 13% faster and accept()
gets up to 30% faster (GCC 13 and clang 18 on x86-64, Apple clang 21 on
arm64). Minified input is unchanged within noise.

* support JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7396) diff creation

The JSON merge patch document format describes the set of modifications
to a resource's content, that more closely mimics the syntax of the
resource being modified.

However, and in contrast to JSON Patch (RFC 6902), a JSON Merge Patch
cannot express certain modifications, e.g., changing an array element
at a specific index, or setting a specific object value to null.
The null value in a JSON Merge Patch is used to remove the key from the
object.

The diff algorithm is not part of the RFC 7396, but it was tested
against all examples provided, plus additional cases on how null values

message:
* Stop the BON8 writer overflowing the stack on deep values

to_bon8() recursed once per nesting level, so a value the iterative
BON8 reader accepts (e.g. ~24k nested one-element arrays) crashed on
the way back out. #5781 bounded the CBOR, MessagePack, and UBJSON/BJData
writers, but BON8 was merged before it and was not covered.

Apply the same scheme: recurse for the first recursion_depth_limit()
levels, then finish the value with write_bon8_iterative, which keeps
the open containers on a heap stack (reusing binary_container_frame)
and writes the 0xFE closer when it leaves a container with more than
four elements. The output is byte-for-byte unchanged.

the 0xFE closer and the marker computation. Share those parts and branch

* Unflatten in time and memory linear in the pointer depth

#5443 made unflatten() decide between arrays and objects independently

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
* Flatten deeply nested values without recursing per nesting level

json_pointer::flatten() called itself once per nesting level, so
flatten() on a value nested deeply enough exhausted the call stack.
#5547 and #5548 fixed merge_patch() and diff() from #5393, but flatten()
was left out.

flatten() now walks the value with an explicit stack and keeps the path
in one buffer that grows and shrinks with it. It has a single code path
and no depth limit: the old version built a new path string per child,
so the iterative one is no slower on shallow values and much faster on
deep ones. The output, including the order of an ordered_json result,
is unchanged.

message:
* Make std::hash<basic_json> consistent with operator== for numbers

operator== converts between number_integer, number_unsigned, and
number_float before comparing, so json(0), json(0U), and json(0.0)
all compare equal. hash() folded the specific value_t into the
result for each of the three numeric cases, giving each a distinct
hash and breaking the standard Hash requirement that a == b implies
hash(a) == hash(b). A std::unordered_set could therefore hold all
three as separate elements even though they compare equal.

hash() now treats all three numeric variants the same way: it
converts the value to number_float_t and combines it with a single
shared type tag, so any two numbers operator== considers equal hash
identically regardless of which internal type actually holds them.

Updated the accompanying test to check this consistency directly
(including via an actual unordered_set) instead of asserting that 0,
0U, and 0.0 hash differently, since that assumption was the bug.
Also corrected the function's own doc comment and the std::hash API
docs, which described the old behavior as intended.

Fixes #5400

message:
* Stop binary writers overflowing the stack on deep values

to_cbor, to_msgpack, and to_ubjson recurse once per nesting level.
The parser is iterative, so a value the library accepts can crash on
the way back out.

Keep the existing recursive path for the first 128 levels and finish
anything deeper on a heap stack. Output is unchanged. BSON is left
alone because its extra size walk is a separate change.

Rebased onto the value-type output sink. The heap frames now initialize
every member, which is what -Weffc++ was rejecting.

See #5392.

Signed-off-by: ayush-singh-0601 <singhayush062006@gmail.com>
(cherry picked from commit cf65ac438f5d43aa9a5cbf3f25c0d20fac51d4ae)
Signed-off-by: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>

* Redesign the iterative binary writers around a shared recursion depth limit

Address the open review on the non-recursive CBOR/MessagePack/UBJSON/BJData
writers (#5518):

- Delete the CBOR array/object prefix helpers; both the recursive and
  iterative paths call write_cbor_head(), which already existed on develop.
- MessagePack: share one write_msgpack_array_prefix()/write_msgpack_object_prefix()
  helper per container kind between the recursive and iterative paths, both
  going through to_msgpack_length() so an over-long container throws
  out_of_range.412 identically either way.
- Reuse detail::recursion_depth_limit() instead of a separate constant, the
  same bound serializer::dump() and write_bson_document() already use.
- Redesign the frames after bson_frame/dump_frame: only a container with
  elements is ever pushed, its header is written at the point it is pushed,
  and the iterator is set in the frame's constructor instead of a
  default-then-assign two-step with a since-removed "started" flag. The
  UBJSON frame keeps only the value pointer, the per-element prefix_required
  flag, and the iterator; write_closer and is_object are no longer stored,
  since the former is always !use_count (use_count is constant for the whole
  document) and the latter follows from value->is_object().
- Factor the BJData ND-array shape check into is_bjdata_ndarray(), used by
  both the recursive object case and the iterative pushing logic.
- Give the frame classes the GCC -Weffc++ treatment already used for
  diff_frame: a noexcept converting constructor plus the five special members
  defaulted with no explicit noexcept.
- Fix two @ref self-references in write_cbor/write_msgpack/write_ubjson's own
  doc comments to point at the public to_cbor/to_msgpack/to_ubjson/to_bjdata
  API instead.
- The iterative object-key write for CBOR/MessagePack now runs the same
  strict-mode check_utf8() against the parent object as diagnostics context
  that the recursive path already ran, so the two paths raise identical
  diagnostics across the switch-over.
- Rewrite the tests: round trips instead of a bare size check, byte-exact
  comparisons against the recursive output at depths around the bound, a
  deep object and a BJData ND-array past the bound, a deep discarded value
  (type_error.321), and the OSS-Fuzz 566583014 CBOR/MessagePack regression.

iteratively and is covered separately by #5553.

author: Niels Lohmann <mail@nlohmann.me>
message:
With JSON_BRACE_INIT_COPY_SEMANTICS enabled, single-element brace
initialization from a JSON value decided whether to copy the value or
build an object by inspecting the value's runtime shape: a two-element
array whose first element is a string, such as ["key", 42], was turned
into an object instead of being copied. This made the behavior depend
on the element's content, and it did not distinguish an existing value
of this shape from a nested braced pair written in the source, such as
the inner {"key", "value"} of {{"key", "value"}}.

json_ref now records whether it was constructed from a braced list
(true only for the std::initializer_list<json_ref> constructor used
for nested braced lists) or from a value. The initializer-list
constructor uses this to copy or move a single non-braced-list element
before deciding whether the list describes an object, so a JSON value
is always copied regardless of its shape, while a braced pair written
in the source still creates an object.

Fixes #5662.

hunk_contexts: inline bool operator<(const value_t lhs, const value_t rhs) noexcept
message:
The mixed number arms of JSON_IMPLEMENT_OPERATOR cast the integer to
number_float_t before comparing. Past the float's mantissa that cast is lossy:
2^63-2 and 2^63-1 both round to 2^63, so each compares equal to that float
while differing from each other. Equality is therefore intransitive and the
ordering is not a strict weak ordering, which makes std::sort over such values,
or using them as keys in std::set or std::map, undefined behavior.

Compare the two exactly instead. The integer's range is a power of two the
float represents exactly, so a float outside it is ordered by magnitude alone;
inside it, truncating the float is exact, and the integer parts and then any
fractional part decide. The helper hands back a pair whose comparison with the
original operator reproduces that ordering, which keeps every operator's return
type as it was, including partial_ordering for the spaceship.

A NaN operand is returned in both members, so NaN stays false for the
relational operators and unordered for <=>. Values a float represents exactly
still compare equal, so json(1) == json(1.0) is unchanged.

Signed-off-by: qatcod <79017227+qatcod@users.noreply.github.com>
subject: Compare integers with floats exactly instead of widening the integer (#5459)
